transcript:
Header:
- Title: Optimize walkthrough — concurrency & prefix/KV cache cost modeling with Aurora Analytics
- Date/Time: 2025-05-21 11:00 AM PDT (recorded)
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tom (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO), Aisha (Head of MLOps), Natalie (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood ran through Optimize recommendations focusing on batching windows, KV / prefix cache strategies, and a cost model comparing hosted vs dedicated with concurrency targets. Customer asked about cold-starts, KMS encryption, and how prefetch impacts latency at 99th percentile. Several follow-ups: share spreadsheet, run pilot, provide SOC2/KMS docs.

Topics:
- workload shape and concurrency profile
- prefix vs KV cache tradeoffs
- batching window sizing and tail latency
- cost model assumptions (token mix, cache hit rate, quantization)
- dedicated pool pilot and SLOs

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Liam (Aurora): Yeah loud and clear. Thanks, Maya. We got Aisha and Natalie on too.
[00:08] Aisha: hi, sorry slight delay, on mobile.
[00:11] Tom (Redwood): Great — I'll share my screen in a sec. Quick agenda: we want to walk the Optimize cost model, show how prefix/KV caching and batching affect unit costs, then talk pilot options. Sound good?
[00:20] Natalie (Aurora): Yep. Our main goal is to figure out how to keep p99 < 400ms for interactive explorer while not blowing budget.
[00:27] Maya: Perfect, that’s the anchor. Tom, over to you.
[00:31] Tom: Alright sharing. I have the Aurora_poc_costs_v1 spreadsheet up, plus a small synthetic trace we used to simulate 1k rps distributed over top endpoints. Note — the numbers are illustrative, we'll run it against your real trace once you send it.
[00:45] [00:46] (screen share starts)
[00:49] Tom: First slide — workload shape. This is the request size distribution: 70% short prompts (~30 tokens), 25% medium (~120 tokens), 5% long (>=512). Concurrency spikes during business hours to ~450 simultaneous streams.
[01:10] Aisha: that lines up with our internal telemetry, though our long tail is slightly higher on weekends.
[01:15] Tom: Good to know. Next — baseline: hosted single-stream with no prefetch or KV cache. Average cost per 1k tokens is X (we show a number) and p99 sits at 760ms under bursts.
[01:30] Liam: So that's a bit higher than we need. Where do the biggest wins come from?
[01:34] Tom: Two levers — batching and caching. With batching we can amortize compute across tokens; with prefix/KV cache we avoid recomputing early layers for repeated prefixes.
[01:45] Maya: quick note — in Redwood Optimize we recommend a hybrid: KV cache for repeated prefixes where you have many similar prompts (search, autocomplete), and prefix cache for very stable start sequences. Prefetch sits in front to warm the KV.
[01:58] [02:00] Natalie: How does prefetching affect cold-start costs? If we prefetch too aggressively do we blow up GPU occupancy?
[02:06] Tom: Good Q. Prefetch has a policy surface: prefetch threshold (how many concurrent requests with the same prefix) and TTL. We model prefetch as additional background requests that run at low priority — they consume cycles but reduce p99 for real traffic. In the spreadsheet we show a 3% increase in GPU utilization for a 25% drop in p99 tail.
[02:29] Aisha: 3% utilization for 25% p99 improvement is attractive. What's the hit on per-token cost?
[02:34] Tom: It depends on hit rate. If KV hit rate moves from 0% to 60% on your 30-token short queries, token compute reduces significantly — cost per request can drop ~35% in that bucket. Overall per-token savings in our sim was ~18% after factoring prefetch overhead.
[02:53] Liam: When you say KV hit rate — that assumes identical key lookups. Our prompts are templated but have user names and IDs in them. How do we make keys effective?
[03:01] Tom: Two approaches: normalize prompts to canonicalized prefixes (strip user-specific tokens) and use hashed keys for relevant prefix lengths. We typically see best ROI when canonicalization keeps the semantic part and removes identifiers — that's something Aisha's team would own in transformation layer.
[03:17] Aisha: yeah we can do that, it's extra engineering but doable.
[03:21] [03:22] Maya: Another practical point: you can set multiple cache granularities at different prefix lengths. Short prefix cache (e.g., first 20 tokens) covers many queries; deeper prefix for sessions where you expect long reuse.
[03:34] Natalie: Are there any correctness or freshness issues? We have dynamic content that changes per minute.
[03:38] Tom: TTLs and eviction policies address that. You can set conservative TTL for dynamic endpoints; for stale-tense content you might not use caching. Redwood's console also exposes hit-rate dashboards so you can tune live.
[03:50] Liam: Ok — what about dedicated pools? If we reserve capacity does that change cost math?
[03:55] Tom: Yes — Dedicated reduces per-token price and removes multi-tenant variability. In the spreadsheet we include a dedicated scenario with reserved 8x A100-equivalent GPUs. In that model, per-token cost drops due to higher statistical multiplexing and no host-level overhead, but you pay reservation even during off-peak. So the breakeven depends on utilization.
[04:15] Aisha: What's the breakeven utilization for dedicated in your sim?
[04:18] Tom: For Aurora's profile it was around 35% sustained GPU utilization. Above that, dedicated with Optimize rules (aggressive batching + caching) looks better. Below that, hosted with autoscale was cheaper.
[04:29] [04:30] (slight cross-talk)
[04:33] Liam: How do you simulate batching? Our tail latency is sensitive — bigger batches can push p99 up.
[04:38] Tom: Right, batching window sizing is key. We model continuous batching: a short wait (5-25ms) to accumulate tokens, then dispatch. For your mix we found ~12ms window captured enough short requests to improve throughput while keeping p99 within SLO. We also simulate max batch sizes and adaptive headroom to cap latency.
[04:58] Natalie: Are quantized models in the calc? We use int8 for some endpoints.
[05:02] Tom: Yes — the cost model toggles quantization level. Quantization reduces GPU compute per token and often reduces latency slightly, but can increase number of steps for some models if quality drops. We included a quality adjustment factor — we recommend running quality evals against your prompts.
[05:20] Maya: On that note, Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per model and per route; it's not one-size-fits-all.
[05:27] Aisha: Security: we need to ensure KMS + customer-managed keys for private deployment. Does prefetch or caching touch plaintext data?
[05:33] Tom: Great question. Cache keys are opaque hashes; cached tensors on the serving side are encrypted at rest and in transit. For Private deployments you can use customer KMS/HSM. Prefetch is treated like any other request — we support encryption and audit logs. We'll share the SOC2/KMS integration note.
[05:52] Liam: And retention — logs and caches — how long do you keep them?
[05:56] Maya: Configurable. On hosted we default to minimal retention for KV indices, and audit logs per your policy. For Private you control retention. We'll include the retention matrix in the docs.
[06:06] [06:10] (Tom scrolls spreadsheet)
[06:12] Tom: Now I'll flip to the cost breakdown: compute, memory, storage for KV indexes, prefetch overhead, and network egress. For most interactive services the compute is the biggest driver. We show that adding KV cache reduces total compute by offloading prefix computation to cached accelerators.
[06:30] Aisha: What's the memory footprint of the KV cache for, say, 10M unique prefixes?
[06:34] Tom: It depends on key length and tensor size. Ballpark: 10M keys with 128-dim vectors ~ allow ~ several hundred GB. We typically shard the index and use TTL to keep hot working set small. Also, you can choose a cold-store for long-tail keys.
[06:52] Natalie: So if we keep hot set to ~2M keys that's more reasonable?
[06:55] Tom: Yes + good TTL policies. In the spreadsheet we model shard counts and estimated persistent storage cost.
[07:04] Liam: You mentioned adaptive headroom earlier. Can you explain?
[07:07] Tom: Sure — adaptive headroom is a dynamic policy that leaves spare capacity to absorb spikes. Instead of running GPUs at 98% steady-state, we keep a target headroom (e.g., 20%) which reduces p99 risk during sudden bursts. For dedicated, headroom means you over-provision the pool a bit; for hosted you rely on fast fallback to other regions/variants.
[07:26] Aisha: That seems safer. How does that affect cost?
[07:29] Tom: It increases reserved capacity cost slightly, but prevents expensive degraded scenarios. In Aurora's sim we set headroom to 15% and it increased cost by ~6% but reduced incident risk materially.
[07:41] [07:42] (Maya types in chat: link to cost sheet)
[07:45] Maya: I just dropped the cost sheet in chat: link: https://redwood.app/shared/Aurora_poc_costs_v1.xlsx (note: link tokenized)
[07:53] Liam: got it, thanks.
[07:55] Tom: Now a quick demo of the Console: Optimize suggestions. Here you can load a route, and we surface suggested batching windows, KV prefix lengths, and expected cost delta with confidence bands — that sim you see is synthetic but similar to your shape.
[08:12] [08:13] (screen: Console UI)
[08:17] Tom: See this UI: suggested 12ms batching, prefix cache length 20 tokens, KV prefetch threshold 3 concurrent similar prefixes. Clicking 'apply' opens a canary rollout config.
[08:28] Aisha: If we apply canary will it automatically fall back to baseline on SLA breach?
[08:32] Tom: Yes — rollouts have automatic rollback triggers based on p99 or error rate. You can also set staged traffic percentages.
[08:38] Natalie: How intrusive is the client change for canonicalization?
[08:41] Tom: Minimal — you typically normalize at the API gateway or a transformation layer. We also support server-side canonicalizers as a managed transform, but that's more of a private deployment option.
[08:54] Liam: Ok. Security again — how do we verify that prefetch requests are not logged in plaintext? Our auditors will ask.
[08:59] Maya: We'll include exact encryption guarantees and logs policy. Prefetch requests are treated as the same class as normal inference calls; logs can be suppressed for prefetch endpoints and all persisted artifacts are encrypted.
[09:10] [09:12] (Tom switches slide to pilot plan)
[09:14] Tom: Proposed pilot: 2-week pilot using a dedicated pool (4 GPUs) with our Optimize defaults. Day 0: baseline capture. Day 1-3: tune batching + caching with your traces. Day 4-10: ramp to 25% of production traffic for benchmark. We'll measure cost per 1M tokens, p50/p95/p99, and KV hit rates.
[09:32] Aisha: Who runs the pilot? We need SE involvement and access controls.
[09:36] Tom: SEs run the config and Redwood Ops assists with pool provisioning. For Private deployments you'll run with your infra team. We'll provide an access matrix for the pilot.
[09:46] Liam: What's the expected uplift if we hit 60% KV hit rate and 12ms batching?
[09:51] Tom: For your mix — about 22-28% cost reduction and p99 improving from 760ms to ~320-380ms. Again dependent on canonicalization quality.
[10:04] Natalie: Are there specific models that work better with prefix cache?
[10:07] Tom: Smaller models with caching friendly attention patterns show larger relative gains; very large models with huge kv states also benefit but storage costs grow. We include per-model profiles in the catalog.
[10:19] [10:20] Liam: Any gotchas we should watch for?
[10:23] Tom: Watch for key explosion from personalization; ensure canonicalization. Also watch for stale responses if TTLs aren't tuned. And validate quality with your eval sets to ensure quantization + kv combo doesn't introduce regressions.
[10:37] Aisha: For evals, can Redwood run them or do we run in-house?
[10:41] Maya: Both. We recommend we co-run initial evals, then hand off tooling so you can run continuous checks. We'll supply the eval harness and dashboards.
[10:50] Liam: Let's talk pricing — do you provide detailed pricing per-token and per-kv-store?
[10:54] Tom: Yes the cost sheet lists compute $/token, storage $/GB-month for indexes, and an amortized prefetch cost per hit. For sales pricing we'll follow the pricing tiers in your quote. For dedicated we provide a reservation fee plus usage breakdown.
[11:08] Natalie: Is network egress significant for cached hits?
[11:11] Tom: Usually not — cached hits avoid full model output and are mostly internal memory ops. For some architectures we still ship partial tokens; that's in the model profile.
[11:19] Aisha: If we wanted to try a hosted + dedicated hybrid (hot routes on dedicated, cold on hosted) is that supported?
[11:24] Tom: Yes — smart routing supports route-level policies. You can pin latency-sensitive endpoints to a dedicated pool and route low-priority batch jobs to hosted.
[11:33] Liam: Awesome — that may be our path. Next steps — I think we should: 1) get the real traces to you, 2) get the SOC2 + KMS docs, 3) run the 2-week pilot.
[11:43] Maya: Exactly. I'll send the spreadsheet and SOC2/KMS docs today. Tom will prepare pilot config.
[11:48] Tom: I'll also draft the canary rollback thresholds you can review.
[11:51] [11:55] (short wrapup)
[11:56] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send Aurora_poc_costs_v1.xlsx, SOC2/KMS note, and pilot run plan. Aurora to send 48h request traces and confirm SLOs. We'll aim to kick pilot first week of June.
[12:08] Liam: Sounds good. Appreciate the clear numbers and practical knobs.
[12:11] Aisha: thanks all.
[12:12] Tom: Thanks — I'll follow up in email and chat with the config files.
[12:15] Maya: Bye everyone.
